Please don’t misunderstand the intent of provocative operator. There is a hole that needs to be filled, one that meets the needs of small to mid level businesses. Someone will develop a kitted system that they can sell up and down the street to stand up businesses rapidly and develop methods that grow that software solution over time. That system would bridge levels 0-5 in a variety of ways to grow the “Business”. I find that systems integrators, in the traditional sense solve a small problem, move on and continue to solve more pieces down the road, even the ones they create. That doesn’t interest me personally. It’s rare that integrators I have met ask the core basic question of how does technology make me more money and enable me to scale and support a M & A strategy. 

I am very intrigued by the prospect of engaging AWS to build that system because their horsepower could leverage our collective experience to do something novel and create residual income that growths in a vertical and horizontal manner in a very short time horizon. We need horsepower alignment.

Amen brother…….who else does that? I want to grow vertically and horizontally! With the right partners and insight, we can do that AND fill the space no one else chooses to participate in! 

Domination!!!!!!

Liked “Ok, I like that. We’re not just here to do a project then leave you with the pieces to deal with later. We’re here to help you mature as a manufacturer. Part of that is tech transformation. Part of that is business transformation. We’re the whole package.”

When we go head to head in a bid with another SI AND we tell them we want to grow their business and have an integrated solution to do so and we don’t care about billable hours because it’s our design we are deploying, and we are LEAN as hell……..that’s how we differentiate. Moreover, we solve their business challenges not just “what’s in their myopic scope”, we can win big with that approach. 
Low costs to implement l, rapid to deploy and business driver centric. That’s who I am purporting we need to be to dominate. 

I don’t feel like any of us signed up for this to be average or even above average. There is a once in a lifetime opportunity for us to close a gap for American manufacturing and if we do not do it someone else will. I will be damned if it’s someone else! Even if it takes a few well focused Canadians to help make that happen!

For me, I am particularly interested in doing good, making the world better. I’m not sure I have a particular area that I care about, nor really any expertise that I can claim to apply. Sustainability on a broad basis appeals, solar and renewables is easiest to claim interest, but I’m not sure I’m any less interested in AgTech or LifeSci… but somehow I want to be doing good and have it a compass to measure against any opportunities/distractions. I’d rather not be everything to everyone, I just don’t quite know how to pick :-)

My daughter (former HR director at Papa & Barkley), introduced “Unplugged” which was 2 weeks of paid time off whereby the company shut down for a week, twice a year and no one was allowed to communicate about work related anything. They had to self monitor, but since everyone was away from work and no production taking place it was successful. She proposed it because they were routinely working 7 days a week for weeks in end. In the end, it was written about in trade journals very favorably, and was held up as an industry best practice and allowed them to attract talent. So your point is not lost with me Ryan.

 I believe we are in the right track with the model, as it shows the deficiency between investment and income for an integrated solution that eliminates the administrative burden on the small to mid size manufacturers.   We have several potential pathways and our fork in the road is a traditional path vs a non conventional path. A blended model with service contracts to initiate a new customer rollout followed by residual income with options to add additional service contracts to the same installed base, while adding new is the one I favor. It’s a slower burn, but ends up with a company that has a much higher evaluation at the end, and not subject to the same macro market drivers that other SIs are subjected to. By that I mean, when capital dries up in a down market, capital projects are the first kill, followed immediately by cancellation of contractors. I have seen it many times over. What never happens is that businesses yank out installed systems that drive their daily business. That’s my perspective. 
The key to this model is the strategic partnerships, which act as a JV for mutual benefit.
